title: I added spreading fire and structural destruction to my browser-based FPS, and now entire buildings can burn down
author: Affectionate_Tie6915
selftext:
Been working on a pretty big update for my game, East Bank, and figured I'd share some of the progress.

One of the things I've been working on is making fire an actual part of the environment rather than just a particle effect. Fire spreads between combustible materials, burns through wooden floors, destroys furniture, and leaves behind the concrete and brick structure of buildings. Smoke accumulates along ceilings and escapes through windows, and NPCs will actually try to avoid burning areas.

The entire city is built using 20 cm voxels with structural physics, so destroying enough of a building's support causes it to collapse.

I've also added drivable gun trucks, flyable helicopters, AI-controlled vehicle gunners, and parachuting.

The most recent update introduces a dynamic day/night cycle and weather system, including thunderstorms, wet surfaces, puddles, lightning, and nighttime lighting throughout the city.

It's all running directly in the browser using Three.js, which has made working on the performance side of things particularly interesting.

Still a lot of things I want to improve, but it's slowly becoming the kind of sandbox I originally envisioned.

Would be interested to hear what you guys think of the destruction and fire mechanics, or what you'd like to see added next.

The game is free to play in your browser, with optional paid multiplayer if you want to play with your friends

[https://eastbank.fly.dev/](https://eastbank.fly.dev/)

comments.author: gpubattle
comments.body:
I am also building a FPS game on three.js + WebGPU, so I have spent a ton of time optizming the preformance.

After trying it out the preformance for a voxel style setup should not be this intensive and asked my AI model what they did with loop testing on the computer locally what to focus on so here is a prompt.

Feed this prompt and it will walk through all the steps to improve the preformance like crazy.

Prompt-------------------

You are helping optimize "East Bank", a browser FPS built on three.js with a 20 cm voxel city, structural physics,

spreading fire, smoke, vehicles, weather and a day/night cycle. Goal: much faster load times and smooth frame

times (a steady 60+ fps with good 1% lows) on mid-range and laptop GPUs, without making the game look worse.

Work in measured steps. Never optimize something you haven't measured first.



STEP 1: MEASURE (do this before changing any code)

\- Add a small perf overlay: frame time, CPU ms per frame (main thread), GPU ms per frame (WebGPU timestamp

  queries, or EXT\_disjoint\_timer\_query on WebGL), draw calls, triangles, JS heap, and how often a frame takes

  longer than 33 ms.

\- Split CPU time per system, timed every frame: voxel meshing, physics / structural checks, fire simulation,

  smoke, AI, vehicles, weather, render submission. Report the top 5.

\- Record a Chrome Performance trace of 30 s of normal play plus one building burning down. Note long tasks,

  garbage-collection pauses and shader compile stalls.

\- Measure load: time to first frame, to playable, total download, the biggest files, and how much time is

  spent parsing / compiling shaders.

\- Write a one-page report: is each scene CPU-bound or GPU-bound, and what are the 5 biggest costs?



STEP 2: RENDERER

\- Use three.js WebGPURenderer (with its WebGL 2 fallback) if not already. Check which backend players actually

  get.

\- Draw calls: one merged mesh per voxel chunk (not per voxel or per block), materials grouped into texture

  arrays, InstancedMesh or BatchedMesh for repeated props, debris and vehicles. Target: under \~1,000 draw calls.

\- Culling: frustum culling per chunk, plus cheap occlusion (skip chunks hidden behind solid ones, or hierarchical

  Z on WebGPU). Distance LOD for far chunks (coarser voxels or merged impostors).

\- Shadows: cascades sized sensibly. Cache static shadow casters and only re-render cascades / chunks that changed.

\- Compile pipelines and shaders during loading (renderer.compileAsync on the scene), never mid-match.



STEP 3: GET WORK OFF THE MAIN THREAD

\- Voxel remeshing (greedy meshing) runs in Web Workers. Send back transferable typed arrays; only "dirty" chunks

  are remeshed, time-sliced so one explosion never costs more than \~2 ms on the main thread.

\- Structural physics / collapse checks run in a worker (or WebAssembly), on dirty regions only, not every frame

  for the whole city.

\- Physics (e.g. Rapier WASM) in a worker if it's a top-5 cost.



STEP 4: MOVE SIMULATION TO THE GPU (WebGPU compute)

\- Fire spread: store burn state, heat and fuel in a 3D or 2D texture / storage buffer and step it in a compute

  shader at a fixed rate, only while something burns. Read only small summaries back to the CPU (e.g. which

  chunks to damage), asynchronously, never a blocking readback each frame.

\- Smoke, sparks, debris, rain and puddle particles: GPU particles (compute update + instanced draw), not per-

  particle JS objects.

\- Weather and lighting effects (wet surfaces, lightning flashes, night lights) live in shaders and uniforms,

  not JS per object.



STEP 5: GARBAGE AND JS COST

\- Zero per-frame allocations in the main loop: reuse vectors, matrices and arrays; no new objects, closures or

  array spreads per frame. Check the trace for regular GC pauses.

\- Pool entities (bullets, particles, debris, NPCs) instead of creating and destroying them.



STEP 6: LOAD TIME

\- Stream the city: load and mesh the chunks near the player first, the rest in the background.

\- Compress: KTX2/Basis textures, Draco or meshopt for models, Brotli/gzip on the server, long-cache hashed

  file names.

\- Split the code so the menu loads quickly and heavy systems (vehicles, helicopters, multiplayer) load on demand.

\- Show the world as soon as the first ring of chunks is ready.



FOR EVERY CHANGE: measure before and after with the same test route (same spawn, same building burned, 60 s),

report CPU ms, GPU ms, average fps, 1% low and load time, and keep the change only if it is clearly better.

Commit one change at a time.
